machine.shared: A development machine, with other work running at times; the A/B runs are alternated for that reason

build.tls: OpenSSL 3.6.5 (bundled, static: linux-ext-libs 1.28); mbedTLS not built on this machine
build.note: CONFIG_DEBUG_TRACK_MEMORY is on (the .config of this machine): every allocation is tracked. A build without it does less work per allocation; that build was not measured here.

method.ab: Written on 2026-10-29, before the tag. 7.29.2 is the C code of main at acb3016f8 (YUNETA_VERSION 7.29.2), measured against 7.29.0, the last release with a study; 7.29.1 changed no C of the libraries or yunos (a comment in helpers.c and a new test, archive_shipping/c_test2.c). The C changes of 7.29.2: the permission check of C_AUTHZ, the date reader of gobj-c (helpers.c), append_content() of timeranger2 (a text append a realtime list cannot parse still reaches the next lists) and its archive, the open of a treedb (its name checked against the ids of its lists), the masking key of C_WEBSOCKET (getrandom() read to the end), publish-stats of C_YUNO, the cn of a certificate in ytls/mbedtls (not built here), M-Bus, archive_keeper and archive_sender, the agent's restart, the controlcenter and the cloners. Measured: the same 47 figures as 7.29.0 -- timeranger2, treedb, C_TREEDB, the rotatory, the inter-yuno events, the TCP and TLS echoes and the BFF logins; the raw event loop and MQTT run none of the changed code and are only in the tag-time figures. The 7.29.0 side is a git worktree of the tag, its kernel libraries, the test module and the benchmarks built against the same .config, compiler and outputs_ext (linux-ext-libs 1.28; 1.27 of 7.29.0 differs only in the openresty build). The two binaries of each benchmark run in rotation, the order turned every round, a sync and a 3 s pause before each run (1 s for the three ctest binaries): 8 rounds. Round 3 was slow on both builds at once (the appends 35% slower on both, the treedb 40-50% slower on both, during one minute of other work on the machine); it is left out and a 9th round, in the same order, takes its place. Mean +- standard deviation (median), t = the change over its standard error; |t| < 3 is noise. The BFF figure is the mean of the Msg/sec samples of a run, the first one (the warm-up) left out, on both sides. The two figures slower outside their noise (the TCP echoes) and the TLS echo were measured again: 7.29.0 and 7.29.2 alternated for 10 rounds, then a rotation of six builds for 10 rounds -- 7.29.0, 7.29.2, and the 7.29.2 benchmark objects relinked with all the libraries of 7.29.0, or with only its root-linux, its gobj-c or its timeranger2.
method.tag_run: The absolute figures of 7.29.2 are its side of the A/B run (its C code, acb3016f8), measured on 2026-10-29 on the machine of the earlier reports; the raw event loop, the event loop with an append and MQTT, which the A/B does not run, were run at tag time on the same build: 5 rounds, a sync and a 3 s pause before each run. The per-second benchmarks drop their first and last second. The binary sizes are those of the yunos, the agent and perf_yev_ping_pong built from the main tree with the same .config.

story.title: Yuneta 7.29.2: a review round of fixes, at the same speed
story.lead: 7.29.2 is the fixes of a review round: a permission check that took roles from the client's kw, an M-Bus master that could not read a long answer at 2400 baud, the date reader, the archive of retention and its keeper. Against 7.29.0, the last release with a study, 45 of 47 figures stay inside their noise; the two TCP echoes measured about 2% fewer round trips, on code that did not change, and inside their noise when measured again.

hero.text: prices: no figure got slower because of a change. The binaries grow 0 to 8 KB.

tiles: treedb: update a node and save it
story.ab_sub: Each benchmark built from the tree of each release (7.29.0 and 7.29.2), the binaries run in rotation: 8 rounds. A change inside its whisker is noise. Everything is on one axis: the change of the time an operation takes.
story.prices_sub: What got slower, how much, in which release, and what it buys.
story.no_prices: None. Two figures measured slower outside their noise: the TCP echo -1.50% (t = -3.7) and the TCP echo with an append -2.70% (t = -6.5). Neither runs code that changed: the objects on their path have the same machine code, and the functions of the binary moved. Measured again they stay inside their noise, and the 7.29.2 binary relinked with the libraries of 7.29.0 measures as 7.29.0: placement, not code.
story.abs_sub: Absolute figures of the 7.29.2 build (its C code: acb3016f8), measured on 2026-10-29, before the tag, on the laptop above, as its side of the A/B run (the event loop and MQTT at tag time, 5 rounds): one process, one core for the event loop. Mean of the rounds.

ab.label: TCP echo through the full gobj stack
ab.meaning: Round trips of a ~140-byte JSON message: C_IOGATE, C_TCP_S, C_PROT_TCP4H, C_CHANNEL.
ab.method: Each release built from its own tree (a git worktree of the tag 7.29.0 and the tree of 7.29.2, same .config, compiler and linux-ext-libs), the binaries run in rotation, the order turned each round, a sync and a 3 s pause (1 s for the three ctest binaries) before each run: 8 rounds (round 3, slow on both builds at once, left out and run again as round 9).
ab.reason: Placement, not code: every object file on the path of the echo (C_TCP, C_PROT_TCP4H, C_CHANNEL, C_IOGATE, gobj.c, yev_loop, ytls) has the same machine code in both releases; of the code 7.29.2 changes, only append_content() of timeranger2 runs in a benchmark (the echo with an append), and the appends benchmark that runs its loop did not move. 17,672 of the 17,880 functions of the binary moved, about 700 bytes, 412 of them to another 64-byte alignment. Measured again in rotations of their own it stays inside its noise: 7.29.0 and 7.29.2 alternated for 10 rounds, -1.69% (t = -2.0); and in a rotation of six builds (10 rounds), -2.11% (t = -2.3). The 7.29.2 binary relinked with all the libraries of 7.29.0 measures as 7.29.0 (+0.24%), while relinked with only one of them it measures -1.28% (root-linux), -2.50% (gobj-c) or -1.37% (timeranger2): swapping one library whose hot code is the same moves it as much as the release does.
